title: Improving search relevance for implicitly temporal queries
research_question: Can frequency patterns of year-qualified query variants reveal implicit temporal intent and be used to improve ranking for queries whose desired results depend on a year that the user did not explicitly specify?
methodology: The paper mines aggregate query-log frequencies to identify base queries that are repeatedly qualified with different years, without using click, user, or session information. It defines a year-qualified weight and a temporal-ambiguity score measuring how strongly year qualifications dominate other query qualifications. The inferred year distribution and ambiguity score are then used to modify a commercial search engine's document scores according to years appearing in document fields. Evaluation uses 670 web queries with editorial relevance judgments and reports DCG@5 across temporal-ambiguity ranges.

key_findings.finding: The query-log analysis estimated that more than 7% of queries belong to the implicitly year-qualified category considered by the paper.
The proposed mining algorithm can infer implicit temporal intent solely from frequencies of base queries and their year-qualified variants, without click or session data.

Baseline DCG@5 decreased monotonically as queries became more strongly associated with implicit temporal intent, indicating that the commercial search engine performed worse on the most temporally specific queries in this evaluation.

Temporal reordering produced little or negative change for low-ambiguity-score groups but improved the highest temporal-intent group from 7.02 to 7.07 DCG@5, a reported 0.84% statistically significant improvement.
The effectiveness of temporal reordering increased as the estimated confidence that a query had implicit temporal intent increased.

limitations: The method addresses only implicitly year-qualified queries and therefore covers a narrow subset of possible temporal information needs.
The evaluation uses a proprietary query log and a commercial search engine, which limits independent reproduction.
The reordering experiment uses parameters tied to the evaluation period, including a Gaussian centered on the year 2008.
The statistically significant ranking improvement is confined to the group with the strongest inferred temporal intent, while lower-confidence groups show negligible or negative changes.
The method infers temporal intent from aggregate qualification behavior and does not determine the intent of an individual user issuing an ambiguous base query.
The study does not address permissions, source versioning, or changing validity of retrieved evidence beyond year-oriented relevance.
raw_claims: The paper defines an implicitly year-qualified query as one that omits a year even though the user's intent may concern a particular year.
A base query is treated as implicitly year qualified when it appears with at least two distinct year qualifications in the query log.
The mining procedure uses query-frequency information rather than user, click, or session data.
Temporal ambiguity is estimated from the share of a query's qualifications that are years.
The ambiguity measure can also be interpreted as confidence that a query carries implicit temporal intent.
The reranking method boosts documents containing years that are strongly associated with the query.
The evaluation contains 670 web queries with graded editorial relevance judgments.
Baseline DCG@5 is lower for queries with stronger inferred temporal intent.
The largest reported reordering benefit occurs for the least temporally ambiguous query group.
Only the highest temporal-intent group's improvement is reported as statistically significant.
